author: A Robot
objectives: Students will describe the apparent path of Mars across the night sky during a retrograde episode, including the eastward drift, westward loop, and return to eastward motion.
Students will explain why apparent retrograde motion occurs in the heliocentric model as a consequence of Earth overtaking a slower-moving outer planet.
Students will contrast the geocentric and heliocentric explanations of retrograde motion and articulate why the heliocentric model is preferred on grounds of parsimony.
Students will predict when retrograde motion will occur for a given outer planet based on the relative orbital positions of Earth and that planet.
Students will compare the apparent retrograde loops of Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn, and explain why more distant planets produce smaller loops.

modules.description: Observe Mars's apparent looping motion in the night sky against the background stars.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Describe the apparent path of Mars across the night sky during a retrograde episode.
Identify the direction of normal prograde drift versus retrograde loop motion.
instructions: Look up at the constellations of the ecliptic.
Watch Mars's path across the stars over several months.

clips.changeMeaning: Spawn the stars and Mars in the night sky. Set initial position.
clips.narration: Welcome to the night sky. From our vantage point on Earth, we look out toward the ecliptic constellations. Notice Mars, our bright red neighbor, resting against the background of stars.

clips.changeMeaning: Move Mars slowly eastward across the constellations to demonstrate regular motion.
clips.narration: Normally, Mars drifts slowly eastward relative to the stars night after night. This is its prograde motion, a direct result of both planets moving in their cosmic orbits.

clips.changeMeaning: Slow down and reverse Mars's position westward to form the iconic retrograde loop. Show the trail path.
clips.narration: But roughly every twenty-six months, something bizarre happens. Mars slows down, halts, and reverses its direction, looping westward for about two months before stopping and turning back eastward.

clips.changeMeaning: Move Mars eastward again to complete the cycle. Track trail shows full loop.
clips.narration: Finally, it resumes its normal eastward march. For ancient astronomers, this backward loop was an agonizing puzzle. Why would a celestial body reverse its path?

modules.description: Explore how the geocentric model utilized complex epicycles to explain Mars's retrograde motion.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Explain how epicycles and deferents combine to produce backward motion in a geocentric framework.
Discuss the limitations and complexity of the geocentric model as observational accuracy increased.
instructions: Examine Earth at the center of the orbits.
Watch how Mars orbits on its smaller epicycle while moving along the larger deferent.

clips.changeMeaning: Spawn Earth in the center and show the deferent ring representing the geocentric system.
clips.narration: To explain this motion, ancient Greek astronomers developed the geocentric model, placing Earth at the very center of the universe. Let's look at how they accounted for Mars's loop.

clips.changeMeaning: Spawn the epicycle circle and attach Mars to it. Show epicycle labels.
clips.narration: Instead of orbiting Earth directly, Mars was said to move in a small circle called an epicycle. The center of this epicycle itself moved along a larger circle called the deferent.

clips.changeMeaning: Animate the epicycle and deferent rotations to show Mars creating the retrograde loop.
clips.narration: Watch the machinery run. When Mars rotates to the inner side of its epicycle—closest to Earth—its backward speed on the small circle is faster than its forward speed on the deferent. This creates the illusion of moving backward!

clips.changeMeaning: Dim the geocentric model to transition thoughts to its extreme complexity.
clips.narration: While this geocentric model worked mathematically, it was incredibly complicated. As observations improved, astronomers had to stack epicycles upon epicycles to keep predictions accurate, violating the principle of parsimony.

modules.description: Observe retrograde motion from outside the solar system, seeing how the heliocentric model explains it naturally.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Explain apparent retrograde motion as a consequence of Earth overtaking a slower outer planet.
Contrast the simplicity of heliocentric orbits with the complexity of geocentric epicycles.
instructions: Look down at the heliocentric layout with the Sun at the center.
Observe how Earth travels faster on its inner orbit compared to Mars.

clips.changeMeaning: Place the Sun at the center and introduce the flat solar system perspective.
clips.narration: Now let us lift our perspective out of the ecliptic plane to see the heliocentric model, popularized by Copernicus. Here, the Sun sits peacefully at the center.

clips.changeMeaning: Introduce Earth and Mars in their respective circular orbits around the Sun.
clips.narration: Earth orbits at one Astronomical Unit, taking one full year. Mars orbits farther out at one-point-five-two AU, moving slower and taking nearly two Earth years to complete its journey.

clips.changeMeaning: Animate both planets at their proper relative speeds to show Earth catching up and passing Mars.
clips.narration: Watch closely as Earth, moving faster on the inside lane, catches up to and overtakes the slower-moving Mars. There are no epicycles here—just two smooth, elegant circular orbits.

modules.description: Simultaneously observe the heliocentric orbital motion and how it projects Mars onto the celestial sphere.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Trace how a line of sight from Earth through Mars projects onto a background of stars.
Demonstrate that the apparent westward loop occurs precisely during closest approach when Earth overtakes Mars.
instructions: Follow the line of sight stretching from Earth through Mars.
Observe how its movement against the background starfield changes as Earth passes Mars.

clips.changeMeaning: Set up the split view with a line of sight connecting Earth and Mars to a background starfield board.
clips.narration: Let's connect both perspectives directly. We've cast a line of sight from Earth, straight through Mars, pointing all the way to the distant stars.

clips.changeMeaning: Simulate normal relative motion. The projected ray sweeps eastward across the stars.
clips.narration: As Earth and Mars move normally, our line of sight sweeps steadily eastward through the constellations. This corresponds to the normal path we see in the night sky.

clips.changeMeaning: Show Earth passing Mars, causing the projected ray to sweep backward (westward) on the starfield.
clips.narration: But now, watch as Earth catches up and slips past Mars. From Earth's perspective, the line of sight suddenly reverses and sweeps westward against the stars. The retrograde loop occurs precisely when Earth overtakes Mars.

clips.changeMeaning: Complete the overtaking. The ray resumes its steady eastward sweep.
clips.narration: Once Earth is safely past, the line of sight resumes its eastward sweep. Retrograde is a real, geometric perspective effect—not a physical reversal, but an optical illusion of relative motion.

modules.description: Interact with a tabletop-scale representation of Earth's orbit to feel the physical effect of relative motion.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Relate personal relative motion to the apparent displacement of a celestial body against a fixed background.
Deduce that the speed and angle of observation dictate the size of the apparent loop.
instructions: Look at the orbital track on the floor or table.
Drag the blue observer avatar along the circular orbit and watch Mars shift against the background.

components.text: Drag avatar along the blue track

clips.changeMeaning: Spawn an orbit track on the floor and a stationary Mars in front of the user to simulate room-scale perspective.
clips.narration: To truly understand this, let's put you in the driver's seat. Imagine this circular track on the floor represents Earth's orbit, and you are the observer on Earth. Mars is resting stationary ahead.

clips.changeMeaning: Activate interactive prompts instructing the user to observe the background parallax change.
clips.narration: Drag the blue observer avatar along the track to simulate walking in Earth's orbit. Keep your eyes on Mars. Notice how Mars shifts against the distant starfield. When you pass closest to Mars, it appears to shift backward!

modules.description: Compare the retrograde loops of Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn to understand how distance affects apparent motion.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Contrast the scale of retrograde loops for Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.
Correlate a planet's distance from the Sun with the angular size of its retrograde loop.
instructions: Observe the three outer planets (Mars, Jupiter, Saturn) orbiting the Sun.
Compare the angular size of their apparent retrograde paths.

clips.changeMeaning: Bring up the comparative solar system model showing Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.
clips.narration: Do all outer planets retrograde in the exact same way? Let's expand our view to compare Mars with its giant siblings: Jupiter and Saturn.

clips.changeMeaning: Draw attention to Mars's large loop vs Jupiter and Saturn's progressively smaller loops.
clips.narration: Mars exhibits a dramatic retrograde loop of about fifteen degrees. Jupiter, much further away at over five AU, traces a smaller ten-degree loop. Saturn, at nearly ten AU, forms an even tinier loop of only seven degrees.

clips.changeMeaning: De-emphasize the inner orbits to focus on geometry and distance.
clips.narration: This occurs because of parallax geometry. Just like a distant mountain shifts far less than a nearby tree when you walk past, more distant planets subtend a smaller angle as Earth sweeps past them.

modules.description: Interact with the planets to predict and arrange the specific alignment that produces retrograde motion.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Predict the relative configuration of Earth and an outer planet required for retrograde motion to occur.
Identify opposition as the orbital alignment where retrograde motion is observed.
instructions: Drag Mars to the orbital position where retrograde motion would be triggered from Earth.
Look for the alignment where Earth is poised to pass Mars on the inside track.

components.scriptDescription: Verifies if the draggable Mars is in opposition alignment with Earth and Sun. Fires callback on alignment success.

components.text: Drag Mars to the alignment position!

clips.changeMeaning: Present the prediction scene with Earth static. Make Mars draggable.
clips.narration: Let's test your understanding. Here, Earth is fixed on its orbit. Your task is to drag Mars to the position where an observer on Earth would see Mars undergo retrograde motion.

clips.changeMeaning: Show target area feedback as helper.
clips.narration: Remember, retrograde occurs when Earth catches up and passes Mars. Think about where Mars needs to be relative to Earth and the Sun for this overtake to happen. Drag Mars into that sector!

clips.changeMeaning: Lock Mars into the correct opposition position upon successful drag and celebrate.
clips.narration: Excellent job! You placed Mars near opposition, directly aligned with Earth and the Sun. At this closest approach, Earth's faster orbital velocity creates the apparent retrograde loop.

modules.description: Review the five core concepts of retrograde motion covered in this lab.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Synthesize observations, models, linkages, and comparisons into a cohesive explanation of retrograde motion.
instructions: Reflect on how the heliocentric explanation revolutionized our view of the universe.

components.text: 1. Observed Loop: Mars periodically reverses westward.
4. Line of Sight: Proves retrograde is perspective.
5. Outer Planets: Greater distance = smaller loops.

clips.changeMeaning: Show the recap panel and highlight the first learning outcome (Observed Loop).
clips.narration: Let's summarize our journey. First, we observed the historical mystery of the sky—the westward loops Mars traces against the stars.

clips.changeMeaning: Highlight geocentric and heliocentric theories.
clips.narration: We saw how the geocentric model struggled with complex epicycles, while the elegant heliocentric model explained retrograde naturally through smooth circular orbits.

clips.changeMeaning: Highlight line of sight project and outer planet differences.
clips.narration: Finally, we linked both views using a line of sight, and learned that more distant outer planets like Jupiter and Saturn show smaller loops due to parallax geometry.
